name: Digital Twins for Experiments
title: Digital Twins for Experiments
answer: Digital twins for experiments are computational models that mirror a physical laboratory system, such as a bioreactor, spectrometer, or robotic assay line, in enough detail to predict its behavior under different conditions. They span the design, execution, and analysis of experiments, allowing researchers to test parameters, troubleshoot protocols, and estimate outcomes before committing wet-lab resources. The scope includes both equipment-level twins, which replicate a single instrument, and process-level twins, which model an entire workflow from sample preparation to data readout. These twins are used across chemistry, biology, materials science, and clinical laboratory settings. They are distinct from static simulations because they are updated with data from the physical system over time.

sections.body: Digital twins for experiments are computational models that mirror a physical laboratory system, such as a bioreactor, spectrometer, or robotic assay line, in enough detail to predict its behavior under different conditions. They span the design, execution, and analysis of experiments, allowing researchers to test parameters, troubleshoot protocols, and estimate outcomes before committing wet-lab resources. The scope includes both equipment-level twins, which replicate a single instrument, and process-level twins, which model an entire workflow from sample preparation to data readout. They are distinct from static simulations because they are updated with data from the physical system over time.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A digital twin for an experiment typically runs on a combination of local laboratory servers, cloud computing, and edge devices attached to instruments. The physical side relies on sensors, actuators, and laboratory information management systems to stream measurements such as temperature, pressure, absorbance, or motor positions into the twin. The computational side uses standard scientific computing stacks, often including Python or Julia, with numerical solvers and physics-based or data-driven model libraries. Storage and versioning are handled by databases that record both the twin's state and the history of physical runs it mirrors. Network latency and data throughput matter most when the twin is used for real-time control rather than offline planning.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Building a digital twin usually starts with a mathematical or statistical model of the experimental system, derived from first principles, historical data, or a hybrid of both. The model is then calibrated against a set of physical experiments so that its outputs match observed measurements within an accepted tolerance. During use, the twin receives new sensor data and updates its internal state, a process called data assimilation, which keeps the virtual and physical systems aligned. Researchers run virtual experiments by changing inputs in the twin and observing predicted outputs, then use those predictions to select the most informative physical runs. Validation is ongoing: each new physical result is compared with the twin's forecast, and discrepancies are used to refine the model.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Digital twins for experiments raise questions about data ownership, model provenance, and the reliability of virtual results when they inform real decisions. A twin is only as trustworthy as the data used to build and update it, so records must show which physical runs, calibration steps, and software versions produced a given prediction. Access controls are needed because a twin may encode unpublished methods, proprietary instrument settings, or sensitive sample information. If a twin is used to justify skipping a physical control or approving a batch, the basis for that decision should be auditable. Rights over the twin itself, including its model parameters and training data, are often separate from rights over the physical instrument or the experimental results.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Digital twins for experiments are moving toward closed-loop laboratory automation, where the twin not only predicts outcomes but also directly adjusts instrument settings between runs. As more instruments expose real-time data interfaces, twins will become standard components of self-optimizing experimental campaigns, reducing the number of physical trials needed to reach a target. Improved uncertainty quantification will let researchers state how much confidence to place in a twin's recommendation before acting on it. Over time, shared libraries of validated twin components may lower the cost of building a new twin for a common instrument class. The main open challenge is maintaining twin accuracy as experimental conditions drift or as protocols change.
